episodes.title: An 86-minute guide to finding PMF | Rob Snyder (Author, The Power of Pull)
episodes.description:
Rob Snyder is the author of The Power of Pull and writes the newsletter The Physics of Startups. He has advised more than 50 startups on growing from zero to $1 million in ARR, drawing on his own experience as a founder who spent two years pushing a product the market didn’t want before accidentally stumbling onto what actually works. In this episode, we walk step by step through his framework for finding product-market fit, from coming up with an idea to closing your first handful of deals.
We discuss:
1. The PULL framework: Project, Unavoidable, List of options, Limitations
2. Where the best startup ideas come from
3. Tactics for cold outreach and running your first sales call
4. Why Rob advises against design partners
5. Goblin mode: what to do when nothing is working
6. How to apply the PULL framework inside larger companies
episodes.descriptionCN:
罗布·斯奈德 (Rob Snyder) 是《拉力的力量》一书的作者，也是时事通讯《初创公司的物理学》的作者。他利用自己作为创始人的经验，为 50 多家初创公司提供了从零到 100 万美元的 ARR 增长建议，他花了两年时间推出市场不想要的产品，然后意外地发现了真正有效的产品。在本集中，我们将逐步介绍他寻找产品与市场契合度的框架，从提出想法到完成第一笔交易。
我们讨论：
1. PULL 框架：项目、不可避免的问题、选项列表、限制
2. 最好的创业创意来自哪里
3. 冷外展和第一次销售拜访的策略
4. 为什么 Rob 不建议设计合作伙伴
5.妖精模式：什么都不起作用时该怎么办
6. 如何在大公司内部应用PULL框架

episodes.title: Inside the black box of AI: How AI models actually think | Emmanuel Ameisen (Anthropic)
episodes.description:
Emmanuel Ameisen is an interpretability researcher at Anthropic, where he looks inside LLMs like Claude to understand how they think. Before joining Anthropic, he spent years in applied ML at Stripe and Insight, and is the author of Building Machine Learning Powered Applications. His research has produced some of the most striking findings in the field: that models form general representations of concepts, plan many tokens ahead without stating those plans explicitly, and may exhibit something structurally similar to the distinction between conscious and unconscious processing in humans.
We discuss:
1. Why the “next-token predictor” framing undersells how models actually plan and think
2. Why anthropomorphizing AI can actually be the right approach
3. Why models are “grown,” not built
4. What the “J space” reveals about model self-awareness
5. The smooth scaling curve behind what look like sudden capability jumps
6. How interpretability connects to AI alignment and safety
episodes.descriptionCN:
Emmanuel Ameisen 是 Anthropic 的可解释性研究员，他深入研究像 Claude 这样的法学硕士，以了解他们的想法。在加入 Anthropic 之前，他在 Stripe 和 Insight 从事应用机器学习工作多年，并且是《构建机器学习驱动的应用程序》一书的作者。他的研究产生了该领域一些最引人注目的发现：模型形成概念的一般表示，提前计划许多标记而无需明确说明这些计划，并且可能在结构上表现出类似于人类有意识和无意识处理之间的区别的东西。
我们讨论：
1. 为什么“下一个令牌预测器”框架低估了模型实际计划和思考的方式
2. 为什么人工智能拟人化实际上是正确的方法
3. 为什么模型是“成长”的，而不是构建的
4.“J空间”揭示了模特的自我意识
5.看似突然的能力跳跃背后的平滑缩放曲线
6. 可解释性如何与人工智能一致性和安全性联系起来

episodes.title: Why every company now needs to think and operate like a lab team | Josh Woodward (Google Labs, Gemini, AI Studio)
episodes.description:
Josh Woodward is the head of Google Labs, the Gemini app, and AI Studio. He has spent over 17 years at Google and oversees its longest-running and largest labs team, whose products include NotebookLM (now Gemini Notebook), Project Genie, and Flow. His job is to find, experiment with, and scale new AI products, and he has built one of the most distinctive product cultures in the industry for generating ideas, running experiments, and, even more importantly, knowing when to quit.
In our in-depth conversation, we discuss:
1. Why every company now needs to think and operate like a labs team
2. Where the best ideas really come from
3. The “almost possible” framework
4. How to recognize genuine product-market fit early
5. When to kill an idea
6. What skills are rising in value in the AI era
7. Why roles are not actually blurring into one universal builder role
8. How to set up your internal labs team
episodes.descriptionCN:
乔什·伍德沃德 (Josh Woodward) 是 Google 实验室、Gemini 应用程序和 AI Studio 的负责人。他在 Google 工作了 17 年多，负责管理其运行时间最长、规模最大的实验室团队，其产品包括 NotebookLM（现为 Gemini Notebook）、Project Genie 和 Flow。他的工作是发现、试验和扩展新的人工智能产品，他建立了业内最独特的产品文化之一，用于产生想法、进行实验，更重要的是，知道何时退出。
在我们的深入对话中，我们讨论：
1. 为什么现在每家公司都需要像实验室团队一样思考和运作
2. 最好的想法真正来自哪里
3.“几乎可能”的框架
4. 如何及早识别真正的产品与市场契合度
5. 何时扼杀一个想法
6.人工智能时代哪些技能的价值正在上升
7. 为什么角色实际上并没有模糊为一个通用构建者角色
8. 如何组建内部实验室团队

Under his stewardship, OpenAI has shipped some of its most consequential consumer launches: Codex, ChatGPT Work, and most recently, the new Dots personal agent platform. episodes.title: The grief, loneliness, and burnout sweeping through the tech industry right now | Molly Graham
episodes.description:
Molly Graham is back for round two, and this one is even more powerful. Molly has spent more than 20 years helping organizations and the humans inside them navigate growth and change. She’s held leadership roles at Google, Facebook, Quip, and the Chan Zuckerberg Initiative and is the host of TED’s WorkLife podcast (which she took over from Adam Grant). She also runs Glue Club, a leadership community for senior operators, and writes a popular newsletter called Lessons.
In our in-depth conversation, we discuss:
1. Why Molly’s famous “give away your Legos” career advice no longer holds true in an AI world
2. The grief, loneliness, and burnout sweeping through the tech industry right now
3. Why delegating to AI is fundamentally different from delegating to a human
4. The fear narrative around AI job displacement, and why it’s overblown
5. Which Legos you should never give to AI
6. What the best managers are doing right now

在我们的深入对话中，我们讨论：
1. 为什么莫莉著名的“放弃你的乐高积木”职业建议在人工智能世界不再适用
2. 目前，悲伤、孤独和倦怠席卷了科技行业

4. 关于人工智能工作取代的恐惧叙述，以及为什么它被夸大了

episodes.description:
Peter Sellis was the first product manager at Snapchat, where he spent seven years building one of the most beloved consumer products in history. He went on to serve as Head of Product at Discord, where he helped drive some of the fastest user growth the platform had seen. Having left his role at Discord, he gets to be especially real and unfiltered — nothing to promote, no PR, no comms team.
In our in-depth conversation, we discuss:
1. Why Peter designs teams like . . . terrorist organizations
2. What it was really like to manage Nikita Bier
3. Why the median PM is so bad
4. Why Snapchat’s ads business never reached its potential
5. Why growth almost always comes from the core product
6. Peter’s three “oxymorons” of great product management

episodes.title: From Wet Lab to RL Env: 10,000 Drug-Discovery Campaigns in a Weekend — Ian Quigley, Leash Bio
episodes.description:
From a four-billion-measurement Kaggle competition to models that recognize a molecule’s chemist, Leash Bio is testing what AI actually learns about chemistry. Co-founder and CEO Ian Quigley joins Brandon Anderson and RJ Honicky to explain how Leash makes DNA-encoded libraries (DELs) produce clean, reproducible protein–small-molecule binding data—and why collecting the right experiments matters as much as choosing a model.
We go deep on hidden shortcuts in public datasets, Hermes’ comparison with Boltz, and the protein mutations that expose memorization. Ian explains how Leash’s measured chemical landscapes can become a sandbox for reasoning agents, with rapid experimental feedback and thousands of medicinal chemistry campaigns. We also examine the limits of DELs, moving hits toward medicines, the economics of AI drug discovery, and the experimental bottlenecks that still need solving.
We discuss:
• How DNA-encoded libraries use barcodes and sequencing to screen millions of molecules
• Catching DNA-binding artifacts with multiple barcodes per molecule
• Why Leash prioritizes reproducible measurements across many protein targets
• The BELKA Kaggle competition: four billion measurements, around 2,000 teams, and no better than chance on an unseen chemical library
• Clever Hans in ChEMBL: learning who made a molecule instead of the chemistry
• Hermes, simple baselines, careful data splits, and comparisons with Boltz
• Activity cliffs, engineered protein mutations, and models that memorize protein “nicknames”
• Agents reasoning about structure–activity relationships in plain English
• More than 10,000 medicinal chemistry campaigns in a weekend
• Going from DEL hits to mouse PK/PD, and the case for pills on difficult targets
• The Kosuri paradox: if you can collect the data, why do you need the model?
• Experimental know-how, detecting misfolded proteins, and scaling purification

episodes.title: Robots That Predict the Future: Dyna-2 & Physical AI — Jason Ma, Dyna Robotics
episodes.description:
From training a world-action model on over one million hours of human video to deploying robots that fold thousands of napkins daily at Din Tai Fung, Dyna Robotics is pushing physical AI beyond impressive demos and into real-world production. In this episode, Dyna Robotics co-founder and Chief Scientist Jason Ma joins swyx on-site to unpack how robots can learn new tasks from as little as 45 minutes of demonstrations, why predicting the future of the physical world may be the key to general-purpose robotics, and what it actually takes to build robots that work reliably for real customers.
We go deep on Dyna-2, Dyna's million-hour world-action model that combines future video prediction with robot actions, the scaling laws behind human-to-robot transfer, diffusion transformers and flow matching, and why synthetic environments and self-generated training data could unlock the next wave of robotics progress. Jason also explains why Dyna builds its own hardware instead of relying on off-the-shelf humanoids, how agentic harnesses enable robots to execute hour-long workflows, why dexterous hands and missing sensory data remain major bottlenecks, and what separates real commercial deployments from the graveyard of robotics startups. We also cover world-action models versus vision-language-action models, GPT-6 and coding agents in robotics, and Jason's journey from AlphaGo and Penn to NVIDIA, Google DeepMind, and founding Dyna.
We discuss:
- Why Dyna-2 was trained on over one million hours of human video
- World-action models: predicting future video to guide physical robot actions
- Diffusion transformers, flow matching, and real-time robotic control
- How robots learn new tasks with as little as 45 minutes of demonstrations
- Why robotics has no equivalent of the internet and data remains its biggest scaling challenge
- Human egocentric video, robot demonstrations, and cross-embodiment transfer
- Synthetic environments, simulation, and models that generate their own training data
- Why robots need on-device inference, model distillation, and custom hardware
- Why Dyna chose wheeled semi-humanoids instead of traditional bipedal robots
- The hardware bottleneck: why dexterous robot hands still overheat
- Best Western, Din Tai Fung, and the difference between robotics pilots and scaled deployments
- The Bitter Lesson of Robotics: scaling data instead of engineering specialized solutions
- Agentic harnesses and robots executing multi-step, hour-long physical workflows
- GPT-6, coding agents, and AI-generated simulation environments for robotics research
- World-action models versus VLAs, and why vision alone may not be enough
- Jason's journey through AlphaGo, Penn, NVIDIA, Google DeepMind, and the Eureka project
- Dyna's research culture, deployment-first philosophy, and vision for millions of robots

episodes.title: Why AlphaFold Didn't Solve Protein Folding — Pushmeet Kohli, Google DeepMind & Sal Candido, Biohub
episodes.description:
From the Bitter Lesson of AI scaling to the unsolved mysteries of protein folding, Google DeepMind’s Pushmeet Kohli and Biohub’s Sal Candido are rethinking what it takes to build AI that truly understands biology. In this special panel moderated by Brandon Anderson, they explore why AlphaFold’s breakthrough was only the beginning, why scaling compute and data alone won't solve biology, and how the next generation of AI models could transform our understanding of proteins, cells, and human disease.
We go deep on the future of AI-driven biology: finding scaling laws in biological data, the tradeoffs between scientific intuition and general-purpose architectures, why protein structure prediction is far from solved, and what it would take to build predictive models of living systems. Pushmeet reflects on the lessons behind AlphaFold, the limits of human interpretability, and whether future frontier models could understand other AI systems better than we can. Sal explains why protein language models may already contain scientific knowledge we haven't unlocked, how biological modeling must move beyond individual proteins, and why achieving Biohub's mission to cure all disease requires thinking in terms of 10x breakthroughs rather than incremental improvements.
We discuss:
• The Bitter Lesson for biology: why scaling compute and data isn't enough
• Why finding the right scaling law matters more than blindly increasing model size
• How low-quality metagenomic data can improve protein language models
• Why AI researchers optimize for available data instead of the most important scientific problems

Meet George Blackman, a YouTube scriptwriter who got his start writing full-time for Ali Abdaal and has since written scripts for creators from 30,000 to over 10 million subscribers.
This is George's second time on the show. Three years ago, we talked about scriptwriting fundamentals. Since then, George has started writing his own videos with AI, and he's spent most of this year building PlayWriteAI, an AI scriptwriting app with more than 700 people on the waitlist. Building it taught him something most creators haven't noticed yet: AI will tell you, very confidently, that it did ten things it never actually did.
This episode is his full process, from voice memo to a script that's ready to record.
In this episode, we talk about:
• The framework behind every educational hook George writes: target, transformation, stakes
• Why the setups and payoffs inside each segment matter more than the hook
• The ending George puts on every single video, and a twist I want to try on mine
• Where a human still has to make the call, and why AI will keep "improving" your script forever if you let it
By the end of this episode, you will have a repeatable system for writing scripts with AI, and a clearer sense of which parts of the work you should keep for yourself.

Meet Kallaway, the creator behind the Kallaway Marketing channel and the founder of Sandcastles — an AI research tool that helps creators find and validate viral video topics before they ever hit record.
Kallaway started 4 businesses. All 4 failed for the same reason: no one knew who he was. No audience meant no customers, no leverage, no second chances. So he made it his mission to understand how audience growth actually works.
He cracked short-form content at scale after years of building online businesses, and he built the research system he wished he’d had from the start. Now he has over a billion views, a 50% viral hit rate, and he built a tool to help other creators do the same. This episode is the full system.
In this episode, we talk about:
• Content minutes — the framework for mapping how much trust your audience needs before they’ll buy at each price point on your offer ladder
• The modern content stack: why short-form and long-form both need to funnel into email, and why that’s the golden goose
• The 3 metrics that actually matter for content creators — ranked in order of importance, with views coming in third
• A live walkthrough of Sandcastles: channel watchlists, outlier score, deep video analysis, and how to use the MCP to run research through Claude
By the end of this episode, you will have a clear research system for finding validated, high-trust video topics — and a framework for staying creative while using data to de-risk almost everything else.

Riley Brown posted the first TikTok video about ChatGPT the day it launched. It got 20 million views and took him from zero to 200K followers in less than two weeks. Since then, he's built an audience of 1.5 million across platforms, raised $9 million to co-found a vibe-coding startup in San Francisco, and developed a content system so systematic that a single viral video gets reposted across seven accounts every week for the rest of the year.

He also makes a strong case for educational screen-share YouTube videos as the single biggest content opportunity right now, and explains why using AI to write your scripts is, in his words, "suicide."

episodes.title: He got 190K Instagram followers…and regrets it?
episodes.description:
🧪 Join The Lab:
Yoni Smolyar posted a video on Instagram every single day for 508 days. Zero followers to start. He didn't tell a soul. What started as a cringe-avoidance experiment turned into a 500+ video archive, a 190K-follower audience, and a software business that made $10K in its first weekend and hit #1 on Product Hunt. This episode is part origin story, part post-mortem, and part philosophy of short-form content in a world with shrinking attention sapns.
We cover: the psychology of the daily streak (day one is the hardest), why he stopped even though it was working, what he believes about short-form video being a net negative for consumers, the app he built to solve his own screen time problem, and the uncomfortable advice he gave me about ditching my studio setup and FaceTime-ing the internet like nobody's watching.

In this episode, Richard walks through his complete four-phase ideation system—audience identification, outlier research (using five distinct methods), idea remixing, and validation—and backs every step with real examples. episodes.description:
I spent two days touring Intel’s most advanced fab and talking to its technical leadership to understand what the chips of the future will look like.
A lot of what's coming next – gate-all-around transistors, backside power, CFET, hybrid bonding – is hard to follow without actually seeing it, so we made all the awesome animated explainers that I wish I had while I was prepping.
I also asked Intel’s leadership how the semiconductor industry will cope with the enormous shock in demand from AI.
AI compute has grown 3x a year for the last decade, but according to Intel's CTO, Intel could only double leading-edge wafer production with today’s global stock of chipmaking tools.
What kinds of tricks can foundries pull to extend this crossover point where demand surges way ahead of supply?
This was a totally new format for us - hope you enjoy!

episodes.description:
The Home Depot's founding story is like an Avengers movie… if the Avengers got fired, went broke, and stacked empty paint cans ten feet high to look legitimate. After being unceremoniously fired from their previous hardware chain at ages 48 and 35, Bernie Marcus and Arthur Blank took the words of their New York banker Ken Langone (who had also just accidentally caused their firings) to heart: they'd just been "kicked in the ass with a golden horseshoe.” They proceeded to author the greatest compounding story in American retail history, helped by some legendary cameos along the way from Sol Price, Jamie Dimon, and Ross Perot (to name a few). And the ending is as good as any superhero film: from its 1981 IPO to today, The Home Depot has been the single highest-returning equity in the entire US stock market — higher than Apple, Microsoft, Berkshire Hathaway, and everything else!

episodes.description:
In 1984, the Walt Disney Company was worth more dead than alive. Disney Animation — the heart of Walt's famous flywheel — had stagnated for years, bleeding away talent while corporate raiders circled, salivating over offers to sell off the film library to MGM and offload the parks to hotel operators. But what followed instead was the greatest turnaround in media history under Michael Eisner and Frank Wells. Beauty and the Beast. The Lion King. Broadway. Bringing the Disney Vault home on VHS and DVD. And the greatest media acquisition of all time — ESPN.
And then... it all almost fell apart. Again. Euro Disney turned into a money pit. Boardroom and executive infighting ran rampant. Animation descended into a dumpster fire. (Remember Chicken Little? Us neither.) Comcast — Comcast!! — tried to steal the company via a hostile takeover. Out of the chaos, a new generation of Disney management emerged under Bob Iger to stage yet another epic comeback with Pixar, Marvel and Lucasfilm, creating the defining media empire of the 21st century…until the tech companies came along. Tune in for the ultimate Acquired thrill ride: Disney, Part II.

episodes.title: AI Software Factories
episodes.description:
“Clearly there are 100x or 1,000x engineers now. The world hasn’t adjusted.”
— Guillermo Rauch (Vercel)
Guillermo: I’ve been really pilled with this idea of software factories. You used to ship the output directly, and everything inside the company was how good is person A at shipping output B? And now what’s happening is the way that I’m judging you as an engineer is, are you producing the factory that will produce multiplicative outputs B through Z, right?
We used to believe, and it used to be somewhat controversial, that there’s 10X engineers. Now clearly there’s 100X or 1,000X engineers. And the world hasn’t fully adjusted to this.
@naval: I used to get flamed on Twitter for saying there are 10X engineers, because it flies in the face of so much equality philosophy that everyone’s equal. But the reality is, when you’re operating in idea domains—when you’re operating in intellectual domains and virtual digital domains—it’s not even 10X. It’s 100X or 1,000X, and it always has been.
Satoshi, Notch, the guy who invented JavaScript, the Brendan Eichs of the world. John Carmack. These are 1,000X programmers.
Not to even mention if you choose the right thing to work on versus the wrong thing to work on, that’s an infinity difference. And it could just be not necessarily even a better programmer, just one who had a better judgment of what to work on in the first place.
And now obviously it’s less controversial, because of AI leverage.

In this solo episode, I break down how to make money with Meta Muse by mining Facebook groups, Marketplace, and Instagram to match buyers with sellers. The idea came after my wife and I had a baby and the agency we hired for a night nurse admitted it found candidates in Facebook groups. I demo Muse finding night nurses at $30 an hour in Montreal, show how to give it a phone number through Bland AI, and share the Marketplace and Instagram tactics I'd use. I close with my four-level framework for growing a matching side business into a trusted list, a community, and a vertical software company.

• Muse mines public Facebook groups, Marketplace, and Instagram to match buyers and sellers in any niche and city.
• A clean list of names, needs, prices, and trust signals is an asset I own and can sell later.
• Facebook groups, business pages, and IG niche pages look undervalued as Muse agents start crawling them.
• I tell Muse where to look, and Facebook groups gave me the highest quality data.
• My four levels: mine the data, own the list, own the room, then build technology.
• A lean cost structure lets me charge a success fee of a few hundred dollars and keep high margins.
Numbered Section Summaries
1. The Night Nurse Search
My wife and I recently had a baby, and our search for a night nurse led us to an agency. The agency admitted it searched Facebook groups for Miami, South Florida, and New York night nurses, and I realized Muse can do that work today. I expect a thousand-plus millionaires to come out of this era.
2. Matching Buyers and Sellers
Billions of people post needs and offers in Facebook groups, on Marketplace, and on Instagram. I pick a niche, a city, and rules for who I approve, like night nurses in Orlando, and Muse handles the structure, matching, DMs, calls, texts, and booking. The top eBay sellers made millions by finding unique products to sell, and connecting buyer and seller holds the same value here.
3. Clean Data as an Asset
Posts across these platforms vary in quality, so Muse cleans the data into Airtable, Google Sheets, or whatever I use. That list of names, needs, prices, and trust signals compounds into an asset I own and can sell, and I'll cover data brokering in a future episode. Each niche needs its own cleaning approach, starting with what my ICP wants.
4. A Phone Line and Undervalued Pages
People give Muse a dedicated number through Bland AI's Agent Line, a non-VoIP US number with talk and text that I believe costs about $15, so Muse can get a number, call me, reach out to people, and close sales. Facebook groups have about 1.8 billion monthly active users by my estimate, and with millions of Muse agents crawling them, I'd start a group, a business page like a Miami agency for night nurses, or an IG niche page now. Buying Facebook groups may also be an arbitrage, so check Facebook's terms of service first.
5. The Four Levels
Level one is mining other people's groups, Marketplace, and IG, and level two is owning a cleaned, priced, trusted list off platform. Level three is owning the room through your own Facebook group, IG niche page, or Marketplace storefront, and level four is building technology like SaaS, vertical agents, and vertical harnesses that automate the workflow end to end. Muse also works as my content hub for Instagram research, and its lean cost structure lets me charge parents a few hundred dollars where an agency team might have charged thousands.

• Work I do for someone up front, like a launch video or a design fix, starts a conversation in place of a cold email.
• Posts on Reddit, X, and YouTube show tasks people still do by hand, and a small tool can fix them.

Numbered Section Summaries
1. Brag
I start with Brag, a skill that turns your project or a website link into a short launch video with music, motion, and post copy. I use Brag Slim, which is designed for Opus 5.5. You pick vertical, square, or landscape and redo any scene that feels off.
2. Agent Reach
Agent Reach sets up the tools your agent needs to research a topic across YouTube, Reddit, and X. I use it for customer research. I search phrases like "I export it," "I copy this into," and "does anyone know a workaround," then talk to the people behind the posts.
3. Voice Studio
Voice Studio is a desktop app for AI voice work, similar to 11 Labs. It runs local models on your own hardware, so a faster computer helps. It generates speech, works from a recording of your own voice, and dubs video into other languages. I'd start with a short recording of myself, then translate the tutorials behind the three most common support questions, with a fluent speaker checking the result.
4. PPT Master
PPT Master turns documents or notes into an editable presentation, and it accepts your own company template. I'd test it first on a proposal I already wrote, with the private information removed, so I know what a good result looks like.
5. OpenRig
OpenRig organizes coding agents into a team, so one agent builds a change, another checks it, and the work passes between them. It works with Codex and Claude Code, runs on Mac or Linux with Node and Tmux, and changes some agent settings, so read those before you run it.
6. Free Tools
Free Tools is a skill from Corey Haynes's marketing collection. It helps you work out what to build and give away to attract the right customers. A skill is a reusable set of instructions for your agent, sometimes with scripts and examples, so you stop rewriting giant prompts every time.
7. Grill Me
Grill Me, a skill by Matt Pocock, interviews you about an idea or decision in rounds and follows up on your answers. I'd use it before I build something I'm excited about, because that's when I skip the awkward questions.
8. Impeccable
Impeccable, built by Paul Bakaus, gives coding agents specific design guidance once you tell it who the product is for. It has commands like critique, polish, bolder, and quieter. I'd run critique on a page

I watched almost 60 minutes of Sam Altman on stage at OpenAI Dev Day 2026. Out of 20-plus launches, I pick the three or four that I think can make people billions of dollars in aggregate. I break down Dots, OpenAI's personal agent platform, plus the Decisions API, the Agents API with computer use, and Sign in with ChatGPT. I also share my four-step framework for building in this world and two business ideas I hope someone takes. If you want to build a business and make money around AI, this episode is for you.

Key Points
• Dots gives plugin builders a front door to 1.2 billion weekly active users.
• OpenAI is doubling down on plugins to make ChatGPT the app ecosystem for AI.
• Sign in with ChatGPT lets users bring their current plan, so a free core app with paid upsells now works.
• Workflows too niche for OpenAI to build become viable businesses.
• The strongest businesses in this world own the trigger, the action, and the feedback.
• Two open opportunities: real-world work APIs and an analytics layer for agent discovery
Numbered Section Summaries
1. The Launches Worth Your Attention
OpenAI shipped 20-plus features at Dev Day 2026, and I focus on four: Dots, the Decisions API, the Agents API, and Sign in with ChatGPT. I cover GPT 6.1 Soul, Ultrafast, Private Intelligence, and Spaces briefly at the end.
2. Dots and the Plugin Comeback
Dots is OpenAI's answer to Muse by Meta and Instinct. A user asks for help, like fixing a permit or finding a restaurant, ChatGPT understands the job, and it selects a plugin, which is essentially a mini app. By my paraphrase, Sam admitted plugins got mixed reviews before, and now he plans to make them a thing. I think billions of dollars of transactions will flow through personal agent platforms, and maybe trillions over 10 to 20 years.
3. Decisions API, OpenAI's Answer to Jev
The Decisions API is in limited preview. It focuses Luna's intelligence on user-defined questions with finite, predefined answers, so developers can classify content, route requests, or choose an agent's next action. I'm hooked on Jev, and I see UI design as an underserved use case, like finding the highest-converting app store screenshots and direct response websites.
4. Agents API and Vertical Harnesses
The Agents API now supports computer use and brings Codex's multi-agent capabilities, tool search, tool calling, and context compaction into your application. OpenAI runs the infrastructure. If you have great data, a great brand, or deep knowledge of a vertical, I would be playing with this today.

Users can now sign in with their ChatGPT login and use their token allowance on other websites. I compare it to Facebook login, which helped create billion-dollar companies like Yelp.
